overall_summary: Analysis of 40 unique Shorts reveals a clear audience preference for extreme, mind-bending space facts—specifically exoplanets with bizarre weather or materials (e.g., burning ice, diamond planets, and ruby rain). Conversely, psychology and brain-related facts consistently underperform, indicating a need to pivot fully into highly visual, cosmic curiosity concepts.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,055 views), 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (1,023 views), and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (721 views) are the top performers, showing high engagement when titles feature extreme physical properties.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on exoplanet profiles focusing on terrifying environments, precious materials, or impossible physics, using high-contrast visual descriptions.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Saturn's Rings?' (294 views) and 'What If You Fell Into This $26 Nonillion Diamond Planet?' (488 views) outperform standard informational titles.
winning_patterns.action: Frame space facts as direct comparisons to familiar Earth elements or hypothetical 'what-if' scenarios to lower the barrier to entry.

weak_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5-53 views across uploads) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently fail to gain traction.
weak_patterns.action: Phase out general cognitive psychology and brain hacks unless they can be tied directly to a massive survival or evolutionary mystery.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'The Eyeball Planet That Could Harbor Life!' (28 views) and 'This Star Is Older Than the Universe!' (11 views) lack the immediate visual hook of extreme weather or materials.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid purely theoretical or slow-paced astronomical concepts; prioritize high-stakes, violent, or visually spectacular cosmic phenomena.

next_video.concept: CoRoT-7b, a planet where it is so hot that it literally rains rocks into oceans of boiling lava.
next_video.opening_direction: Imagine a world where the oceans aren't made of water... but boiling, liquid lava.
next_video.twist_direction: Because the atmosphere is made of vaporized rock, the clouds condense and literally rain solid stones back down.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful exoplanet weather formula seen in the ruby rain and burning ice videos, keeping the duration under 20 seconds for optimal completion rate.

experiment: Test a 'What-If' space survival scenario focusing on an extreme planet to see if combining the 'What-If' format with exoplanet physics increases average viewer retention.
